1. [Call sites `mcpInvoke(...)` in `/tools/invoke` and `/mcp` routes] — The function is invoked before its declaration only safely because it is a function declaration; no error exists here, but the supplied excerpt is incomplete in the tool output, so an exhaustive character-by-character report cannot be verified from the available file passage.  
2. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/run`] — The endpoint transitions a newly created `pending` task directly to `completed`, but `TRANSITIONS.pending` does not allow `completed`; calling `/run` on a pending task always fails with `illegal transition pending -> completed`.  
3. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/run`] — The endpoint also fails for a `waiting_human` task because `TRANSITIONS.waiting_human` does not allow `completed`, yet `/run` attempts that transition directly.  
4. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/heartbeat`] — The update is not conditioned on task state, lease owner, or optimistic-lock version, so a caller can renew the lease of a task that is paused, completed, failed, cancelled, deleted, or owned by another worker.  
5. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/heartbeat`] — The route ignores database errors and returns `{ ok: true, task: null }` when the task does not exist or the update fails.  
6. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/phase`] — The phase update is not conditioned on task state, lease owner, or version, allowing phases to be changed for terminal, deleted, or concurrently modified tasks.  
7. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/phase`] — The route ignores database errors and emits `task.phase` even if no task was updated.  
8. [Route `DELETE /tasks/:id`] — The update is not constrained by `deleted_at IS NULL` or the task version, so concurrent deletion/state changes can be overwritten without conflict detection.  
9. [Route `DELETE /tasks/:id`] — The delete route ignores database errors, then emits deletion/audit events and returns success even if the database update failed.  
10. [Function `reclaimQuery`] — Reclaiming an expired running task sets it to `pending` without incrementing `version`, creating a lost-update race with `transition`.  
11. [Function `reclaimQuery`] — Reclaimed tasks retain `heartbeat_at`, `phase`, and any other execution fields, leaving a supposedly pending task with stale execution metadata.  
12. [Route `POST /recover`] — The pending-task query uses `.lte("scheduled_at", nowIso())`; rows whose `scheduled_at` is `NULL` are excluded, so newly created unscheduled pending tasks are never returned as schedulable.  
13. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/resume`] — Resuming a paused task sets `scheduled_at` but does not set a lease owner, lease expiry, or heartbeat, despite setting the task to `running`.  
14. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/human-input`] — Resuming from `waiting_human` sets the task to `running` without assigning or renewing a lease, lease owner, or heartbeat.  
15. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/start`] — The endpoint accepts any `owner` value and does not reject an unexpired lease owned by someone else, so a second caller can steal an active task.  
16. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/start`] — The endpoint permits `failed -> running`, as defined by `TRANSITIONS`, without clearing the task’s stored error or stale terminal/execution data.  
17. [Function `transition`] — `const current = String(task["state"]) as TaskState` asserts arbitrary database content as `TaskState`; if the stored value is invalid, `TRANSITIONS[current]` is `undefined` and `.includes` throws a runtime `TypeError`.  
18. [Function `transition`] — The optimistic-lock predicate uses `.eq("version", task["version"])`, while the new value uses `Number(task["version"] ?? 1) + 1`; a task row with a missing/null version attempts to match `NULL` but writes `2`, making the update fail or behave inconsistently.  
19. [Function `transition`] — It updates task state before emitting the state event; if `emit` fails, the endpoint returns an error even though the state transition has already committed.  
20. [Function `audit`] — Database insertion errors are ignored; audit records can fail silently.  
21. [Function `emit`] — Database insertion errors are ignored; event records can fail silently.  
22. [Function `spawnAgents`] — The child-agent insert result and error are ignored, so task creation can return success after creating only the root agent.  
23. [Route `POST /tasks`] — Task creation commits before `spawnAgents`; if agent creation fails, the endpoint returns an error while leaving a created task in the database.  
24. [Route `POST /tasks`] — The idempotency lookup and insertion are not atomic; concurrent requests using the same session and idempotency key can both create tasks unless a database uniqueness constraint independently prevents it.  
25. [Route `POST /tasks`] — `state_data: (body["state_data"] as Json) ?? {}` accepts non-object values such as strings, arrays, numbers, and `null`-adjacent invalid types through an unchecked cast.  
26. [Route `GET /tasks`] — `limit` is passed directly from the query string without validation; negative, zero, non-numeric, or excessively large values can cause database errors or unbounded/undesired queries.  
27. [Route `POST /models/complete`] — `messages` is only checked as an array and its members are not validated; malformed messages can be sent to the model provider.  
28. [Route `POST /models/complete`] — `max_tokens` is converted with `Number(...)` without validating finiteness, positivity, integrality, or bounds; invalid values such as `NaN`, negative numbers, and `Infinity` can be sent upstream.  
29. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`] — The route inserts a tool-call record but ignores insertion errors; if insertion fails, dereferencing `call.id` causes a runtime exception.  
30. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`] — `input` is cast to `Json` without runtime validation, so primitive values can reach property-access operations and tool implementations with incorrect types.  
31. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`] — The advertised tools `sandbox.provision`, `browser.session`, and `artifact.write` have no implementation; invoking any of them always returns `unknown tool`.  
32. [Route `GET /tools`] — The advertised `mcp.invoke` capability is `"mcp"` and `artifact.write` is `"artifacts"`, but `capabilities()` contains neither key, producing an internally inconsistent capability report.  
33. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`, `shell.exec`] — `sandbox_remote_id` is accepted from arbitrary input and is not resolved against an authorized sandbox record.  
34. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`, `shell.exec`] — The command is allowed to be an empty string; the downstream sandbox receives an invalid or meaningless execution request rather than a local validation failure.  
35. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`, `research.search`] — An empty query is passed to Exa without validation.  
36. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`, `model.complete`] — `input["messages"]` is cast without verifying that it is an array of valid chat-message objects.  
37. [Route `POST /agents`] — If `parent_id` does not identify an agent, the code silently assigns depth `1` instead of rejecting the nonexistent parent reference.  
38. [Route `POST /agents`] — The route does not verify that `parent_id` belongs to the same `task_id`, allowing cross-task parent/child relationships.  
39. [Route `POST /agents`] — The route does not verify that `task_id` identifies an existing task before inserting an agent.  
40. [Route `POST /agents/run`] — The route does not catch model-routing failures, so provider errors escape to `dispatch` and return a generic 500 response rather than a route-specific failure.  
41. [Route `POST /agents/run`] — The update result and error are ignored; it can emit `agent.completed` and return `{ ok: true, agent: null }` even if the update fails.  
42. [Route `POST /agents/run`] — The route sets the agent to `completed` regardless of whether the model output is empty, an escalation marker, or otherwise unusable.  
43. [Route `POST /sandboxes`] — The initial sandbox-record insertion result and error are ignored; dereferencing `record.id` throws if the insert fails.  
44. [Route `POST /sandboxes`] — A sandbox is marked `ready` even when the provider response contains neither `id` nor `vm_id`; `remote_id` is then stored as an empty string.  
45. [Route `POST /sandboxes`] — The update result and error are ignored; the endpoint can return success with `sandbox: null` after a failed ready-state update.  
46. [Route `POST /browser`] — A supplied `sandbox_id` that does not exist produces `remoteId = null` and still attempts to create a browser session instead of rejecting the invalid reference.  
47. [Route `POST /browser`] — The initial browser-session insertion result and error are ignored; dereferencing `session.id` throws if insertion fails.  
48. [Route `POST /browser`] — The route marks a session open without persisting the provider’s browser-session identifier, so later browser operations cannot address the remote session.  
49. [Route `POST /browser`] — The update result and error are ignored; the endpoint can return success with `browser_session: null`.  
50. [Route `POST /research`] — Search results are returned as locally built `rows` rather than the records produced by `upsert`; database-generated IDs, timestamps, and conflict-update results are discarded.  
51. [Route `POST /research`] — If `agent_sources.upsert` fails, its error is ignored; the endpoint emits `research.completed` and returns success as though persistence succeeded.  
52. [Function `canonicalUrl`] — It forcibly changes every parsed URL’s scheme to `https`, treating distinct `http` and `https` resources as the same canonical source and potentially generating a URL that does not exist.  
53. [Function `canonicalUrl`] — It removes every `ref` query parameter, even when `ref` is semantically required by the resource rather than tracking metadata.  
54. [Route `POST /mcp`] — The MCP server record is inserted/upserted before connection validation; an unreachable or malformed endpoint remains persisted.  
55. [Route `POST /mcp`] — The `transport` field is accepted but never used by `mcpInvoke`; every server is treated as an HTTP POST JSON-RPC endpoint.  
56. [Route `POST /mcp`] — If `mcpInvoke` fails after a successful registration, the endpoint returns `ok: true` and a warning, causing callers that rely on `ok` to treat an unreachable server as successful registration.  
57. [Function `mcpInvoke`] — It does not validate that `server.url` is an HTTP(S) URL before passing it to `fetch`, so malformed stored values throw at runtime.  
58. [Function `mcpInvoke`] — It assumes all server transports accept one JSON-RPC POST request and one text response; this is incompatible with MCP transports that require initialization, sessions, streaming protocol handling, or a different connection mechanism.  
59. [Function `mcpInvoke`] — For SSE responses, it joins all `data:` lines without delimiters and then parses the concatenation as one JSON document; multiple events produce invalid JSON or corrupted output.  
60. [Function `mcpInvoke`] — It recognizes SSE only when the response body begins exactly with `event:` or `data:`; leading comments, whitespace, BOMs, or other valid SSE fields cause it to treat the entire stream as JSON/text instead.  
61. [Function `mcpInvoke`] — It returns JSON-RPC error objects as successful results instead of detecting and throwing on a response `error` member.  
62. [Route `POST /credentials`] — Encryption key material falls back to `MODAL_PROXY_TOKEN_SECRET`, coupling credentials to a provider token; rotating that token can make all stored credentials undecryptable.  
63. [Function `capabilities`] — `model_primary: Boolean(env("MODAL_BASE_URL") ?? true)` is always `true`, even if the service cannot actually call the primary provider.  
64. [Function `capabilities`] — Capability detection checks only environment variables for Requesty, Exa, and InstaVM, but execution resolves credentials from both environment variables and the credential table; reported capabilities can be false while the functions are operational.  
65. [Function `capabilities`] — `credentials: true` is unconditional even when no master encryption key is configured and credential write/read operations will fail.  
66. [Function `callPrimary`] — The hard-coded fallback Modal URL and fallback credentials are embedded in source, making the deployment depend on static external configuration rather than explicit runtime configuration.  
67. [Function `callPrimary`] — On a non-retryable HTTP response, it throws inside the `try` block and immediately catches that error, then retries until the four-minute deadline; non-retryable 4xx errors are therefore retried repeatedly.  
68. [Function `callPrimary`] — The function has no per-request abort signal or fetch timeout; a single hung `fetch` can exceed the nominal four-minute retry window indefinitely.  
69. [Function `callPrimary`] — A successful HTTP response with missing or malformed `choices[0].message.content` returns an empty string rather than treating the provider response as an error.  
70. [Function `callRequesty`] — The function has no timeout, abort handling, retry policy, or response-shape validation; hung or malformed provider responses can propagate as empty successful completions.  
71. [Function `routeCompletion`] — For code intent, a Requesty failure is silently swallowed and immediately replaced by the primary model; callers lose the reason that the intended coding model failed.  
72. [Function `routeCompletion`] — For non-code intent, an escalation failure is silently swallowed; if the primary output was an escalation marker or empty, the function may make a second primary request without exposing the failed escalation.  
73. [Function `routeCompletion`] — The final fallback primary call is unguarded; its failure escapes and becomes a generic endpoint error.  
74. [Function `looksRefused`] — The refusal detector is a fragile substring list and can misclassify legitimate text containing phrases such as “not supported,” while missing many actual refusals.  
75. [Function `needsEscalation`] — Escalation detection depends on literal substrings only and does not inspect whether the result actually answers the prompt; unusable but nonempty outputs are accepted as primary answers.  
76. [Route `POST /webhooks/:second`] — The request body is parsed before signature validation, so malformed JSON is converted to `{ raw }` and still processed after a valid signature instead of rejecting invalid webhook payload syntax.  
77. [Route `POST /webhooks/:second`] — Webhook events are accepted for arbitrary endpoint names because `second` is never validated against a defined webhook type.  
78. [Route `POST /webhooks/:second`] — The route does not validate that a supplied `task_id` exists before emitting an event referring to it.  
79. [Route `POST /webhooks/:second`] — The handler has no replay protection, timestamp validation, event identifier deduplication, or idempotency handling; a valid signed request can be processed repeatedly.  
80. [Route `POST /leases`] — `ttl_seconds` is not validated for finiteness, positivity, or reasonable bounds; negative, zero, `NaN`, and infinite values lead to invalid or immediately expired lease timestamps.  
81. [Route `POST /leases`] — The read-then-upsert lease acquisition is not atomic; two concurrent requests can both observe an expired/unheld lease and both report successful acquisition.  
82. [Route `POST /leases`] — The upsert result and error are ignored; a database failure can return `{ ok: true, lease: null }`.  
83. [Route `POST /schedule`] — `scheduled_at` is stored as an arbitrary string without validating that it is a parseable timestamp.  
84. [Route `POST /schedule`] — The update result and error are ignored; scheduling a nonexistent task returns success with `task: null`.  
85. [Route `POST /cli`, `ask`] — `ask` accepts no required argument; an empty prompt is sent to the model provider.  
86. [Route `POST /cli`, `exec`] — `exec` accepts no required command after the verb; an empty command is sent to the sandbox.  
87. [Route `POST /cli`] — Splitting commands with `/\s+/` does not support quoting, escaping, or argument boundaries, so commands and arguments containing spaces cannot be represented correctly.  
88. [Function `segmentsFrom`] — The route parser strips only paths beginning with `/api/agent`; if this route is mounted differently or invoked through a base path, endpoint segments are parsed incorrectly.  
89. [Exported `Route` handlers] — The route registers GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE handlers but not PUT, even though `handle` explicitly parses PUT request bodies; PUT requests cannot reach that logic.  
90. [Function `handle`] — Request JSON parse failures are converted into `{ raw }` rather than returning a 400 error; endpoints can then execute with malformed payloads and misleading validation errors.  
91. [Multiple database routes] — Numerous `.maybeSingle()` and `.select()` calls ignore returned `error` values, causing database failures to be indistinguishable from missing records or successful empty results.  
92. [Type declarations and database wrapper] — `db()` casts the Supabase client to `any`-like methods, disabling compile-time checking of table names, column names, response shapes, and query API usage.  
93. [Function `fromBase64`] — Invalid Base64 input throws synchronously from `atob`; decryption callers do not convert this into a controlled credential-corruption result.  
94. [Functions `toBase64` and `fromBase64`] — The byte-to-binary-string conversion is \(O(n)\) string concatenation for encoding and can become inefficient for large values.  
95. [Function `ensureSession`] — If a provided `session_id` does not exist, the function silently falls back to lookup/create by `external_key`, or creates a fresh session, instead of reporting the invalid session reference.  
96. [Function `ensureSession`] — If both `session_id` and `external_key` are supplied but identify different existing sessions, the function returns the session ID match without detecting the conflict.  
97. [Route `GET /sessions/:id`] — The route does not exclude deleted or otherwise inactive sessions, unlike task lookup which explicitly excludes deleted tasks.  
98. [Route `GET /agents`] — Agent listing does not exclude agents belonging to deleted tasks.  
99. [Route `GET /sandboxes`] — Sandbox listing does not filter by task or lifecycle state and provides no pagination, making result size grow without bound.  
100. [Route `GET /browser`] — Browser-session listing has no pagination or task filter, making result size grow without bound.  
101. [Route `GET /credentials`] — Credential metadata listing has no pagination.  
102. [Route `GET /leases`] — Lease listing includes expired leases and has no filtering or cleanup.  
103. [Route `GET /sources`] — Source listing is limited to 200 records but has no pagination cursor or indication that results were truncated.  
104. [Route `GET /artifacts`] — Artifact listing is limited to 200 records but has no pagination cursor or indication that results were truncated.  
105. [Route `GET /tasks/:id/events`] — Event listing is limited to 500 records but has no pagination cursor or indication that results were truncated.  
106. [Route `GET /tasks/:id/stream`] — The stream relies on polling every 1.5 seconds for up to five minutes and opens a database query on every iteration, creating unnecessary database load for each subscriber.  
107. [Route `GET /tasks/:id/stream`] — Exceptions in the stream’s `start` callback are not caught; database errors can terminate the stream without a structured SSE error event.  
108. [Route `GET /tasks/:id/stream`] — The stream does not handle cancellation explicitly; it depends on `request.signal.aborted`, which may not reliably reflect client-side response-stream cancellation in all runtimes.  
109. [Route `GET /tasks/:id/stream`] — If the task does not exist, the stream stays open until the five-minute deadline rather than returning 404 or ending immediately.  
110. [Route `GET /tasks/:id/stream`] — Parsing `after` with `Number(...)` permits `NaN`, negative, fractional, and infinite IDs; the resulting query can fail or behave incorrectly.  
111. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/complete`] — `final_response` defaults to an empty string and is not validated, allowing a task to be completed with no result.  
112. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/complete`] — `final_writer_alias` accepts any string without validating it against known model aliases.  
113. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/error`] — The error code accepts arbitrary JSON, and the endpoint does not validate a nonempty error message.  
114. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/await-human`] — The endpoint creates a continuation token but leaves any existing lease owner and expiry intact, so a worker can retain an active lease while the task waits for human input.  
115. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/human-input`] — The continuation token is only checked when the stored token is truthy; a malformed stored empty token would permit human input without token verification.  
116. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/human-input`] — Human-input payload values are stored without schema validation, so incompatible or unexpectedly large values can be persisted.  
117. [Route `POST /tasks/:id/run`] — The run endpoint does not transition the task to `running` before invoking the model, so concurrent callers can execute the same pending task simultaneously.  
118. [Route `POST /agents/:id/run`] — The agent-run endpoint does not claim or transition the agent into a running state before invoking the model, allowing duplicate concurrent executions.  
119. [Route `POST /mcp/invoke`] — The route permits empty server and method values until `mcpInvoke` fails, instead of validating required request fields.  
120. [Route `POST /tools/invoke`, `mcp.invoke`] — The tool path likewise permits empty server and method values, yielding runtime failures rather than input validation.  
121. [Route `POST /research`] — `num_results` is converted with `Number(...)` without validation; invalid, negative, fractional, or excessive values are sent to Exa.  
122. [Function `exaSearch`] — The parsed API response is asserted as `{ results?: any[] }` without validating JSON shape; nonconforming provider responses are treated as successful empty/invalid data.  
123. [Function `instavm`] — The helper always uses HTTP POST, so any provider operation requiring GET, DELETE, PATCH, or another method cannot be represented.  
124. [Function `instavm`] — The helper has no timeout or abort signal; hung InstaVM requests can hold route execution indefinitely.  
125. [Route `POST /artifacts`] — Artifact path, MIME type, and content are stored without validation or size limits; invalid paths/types and arbitrarily large content are accepted.  
126. [Route `POST /artifacts`] — Artifact insertion is not idempotent and has no uniqueness handling, so duplicate submissions create duplicate records.  
127. [Route `POST /artifacts`] — `emit` runs after successful insertion; if event emission fails, the endpoint can return an error despite having created the artifact.  
128. [Unused constant `TASK_STATES`] — The state list is used only to derive a TypeScript type and is not used for runtime validation of stored state values or request data.  
129. [Unused function `encryptSecret` / `decryptSecret` dependency path] — Credential persistence is tied to runtime support for Web Crypto and browser-style `btoa`/`atob`; runtimes lacking either global will fail at runtime.  
130. [Function `env`] — Accessing `process.env` assumes a Node-compatible runtime; deployment to an edge runtime without `process` causes a runtime reference error.  
131. [Functions using `Buffer`, `createHmac`, and `timingSafeEqual`] — These APIs require Node compatibility, conflicting with code elsewhere that appears designed around web-standard `Request`, `Response`, `ReadableStream`, and Web Crypto APIs if deployed to a non-Node server runtime.  
132. [Function `readCredential`] — Database query errors are ignored; a database failure is treated like a missing credential and can cause misleading “missing credential” errors.  
133. [Route `POST /credentials`] — Credential names have no format restrictions, so arbitrary strings can be used as names and later interpolated into configuration flows without a stable namespace.  
134. [Route `DELETE /credentials/:name`] — The delete result and error are ignored; deletion of a nonexistent credential or a failed deletion returns success and is audited as successful.  
135. [Function `sha256Hex`] — The digest is used only for stored artifact metadata; no retrieval path verifies it, so corruption detection is not implemented.  
136. [Function `handle`] — The method/body parsing supports `PATCH`, but no route branch handles PATCH; every PATCH request is parsed then returns `unknown endpoint`.  
137. [Function `handle`] — The method/body parsing supports `PUT`, but no route branch handles PUT and the exported route does not register PUT.  
138. [Route `POST /tasks`] — `priority` accepts arbitrary finite numeric values, including negative values and values outside a defined priority range.
